title: the lac house
hook: the city starts calling Yudhishthira its future king, and Duryodhana makes his father an offer: a holiday in Varanavata

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Karna's abandonment: a crown, a bow to the old charioteer, an insult at sunset. It follows him into every room.

Talk in the streets of Hastinapura: people are saying Yudhishthira should be king. He's fair, he's truthful, he's Pandu's eldest. Dhritarashtra is blind, so he was passed over before; why should his line rule now? Word reaches Duryodhana, and it burns. The Mahabharata gives him a long, anguished speech to his father: if Yudhishthira takes the throne, the crown will pass down his line, and we and our children will be shut out.
screen: `THE STREETS TALK.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA SHOULD BE KING.` → `DURYODHANA BURNS.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana's plan is dressed up as a kindness. Send the Pandavas away, he tells his father, to the town of Varanavata, where a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva, is under way. Let them enjoy themselves, out of the capital, out of the people's eyes. Dhritarashtra hesitates. Pandu was good to me, he says, and the people love his sons; how can I do this? But he loves his own son, and in the end he agrees. So the old king calls his nephews in and speaks warmly of Varanavata: a lovely town, a festival, go and enjoy it. Yudhishthira sees the purpose behind it, the text says, but he's alone and without friends at court, and he agrees. Then Duryodhana calls a minister named Purochana and gives him the real job. Go ahead to Varanavata. Build a fine house for the Pandavas, out of lac and resin and other things that burn, plastered over so it looks like any house. Treat them well. Earn their trust. And one night, while they sleep, set it on fire. Notice the shape of the plot. Nothing is done in the open. A father is persuaded, a holiday offered, a house built with care. Every step looks generous: a trap made of kindness. And it can't happen without the blind king, who hesitated, and then said yes.
screen: `SEND THEM ON A HOLIDAY.` · `THE BLIND KING HESITATES.` · `PUROCHANA'S REAL JOB.` · `A HOUSE BUILT TO BURN.` · then, large: `A TRAP MADE OF KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Recall a time you went along with something you suspected wasn't right, because it was easier, or because someone you loved wanted it. Don't scold yourself; just look at the moment honestly, the way the story looks at Dhritarashtra, and notice where the hesitation lived.
Purochana, the minister Duryodhana trusted to build a house of lac and resin in Varanavata, and to set it aflame.
Your line: a trap made of kindness. Every step looked generous, and the house is going up. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The bait in this story is a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva; Hindus still worship Shiva as Pashupati, and the Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu carries the name.

tell your nephews what your son wants.

original.note: Sanskrit lākṣāgṛha: the house of lac, built to burn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a house that catches fire by accident.
what it means: a house planned to burn, offered as a kindness, with every step of the plot made to look generous.
what a scholar hears: the plot needs the blind king's consent, and the text shows him hesitating before he gives it.

chat.says: Why did Duryodhana send his cousins to a festival in Varanavata?
options: To get them out of the capital, into a house built to burn.
To reward them for their skill in the arena with a holiday.
To make peace, because the people wanted the cousins to share.
chat.meaning: The holiday was a cover. Purochana was sent ahead to build a house of lac and resin, earn their trust, and set it on fire.
